Hatchlings of the Chihuahuan spotted whiptail (Aspidoscelis exsanguis) emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs with a snout-vent length of approximately 3.0 centimeters [Lb = approximately 3.0 centimeters], a measurement recorded consistently across multiple clutches incubated under controlled laboratory conditions. This modest hatchling size is typical of the Aspidoscelis genus, reflecting an energetic strategy that prioritizes the production of numerous, relatively small offspring over fewer, larger neonates. Shortly after the hatching event, the young lizards begin exogenous feeding, consuming small arthropods as they embark on a period of rapid somatic growth. Juveniles exhibit a distinctive blue tail coloration, a known antipredator adaptation that deflects attacks away from the vulnerable head and torso. Under the stable thermal conditions of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a temperature that approximates the average subsurface soil temperature in their native Chihuahuan Desert habitat during the active season, the progression through critical life history stages has been well characterized. This temperature regime provides a useful baseline for understanding the species’ developmental physiology, as it permits direct comparison of key life history metrics without the confounding effects of thermal variation often encountered in natural field settings.

Under these controlled environmental conditions at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the time since birth at which female Chihuahuan spotted whiptails attain puberty has been determined to be approximately 427 days [tp = approximately 427 days]. This period corresponds to slightly more than fourteen months of post-hatching growth and physiological development, during which the lizards must accumulate sufficient energy reserves to initiate gonadal activation and the complex hormonal cascades associated with reproductive maturity. The onset of puberty in this species is somewhat later than that reported for certain smaller-bodied congeners from more mesic environments, a delay that may be linked to the pronounced seasonal fluctuations in prey availability and the extended periods of winter torpor characteristic of the Chihuahuan Desert ecosystem. Upon reaching this developmental milestone, females begin the process of vitellogenesis and become capable of mating during the subsequent spring activity period. Understanding the precise timing of reproductive maturation is fundamental for constructing accurate population models, as it directly influences the number of annual breeding cohorts and the overall generation time of the population.

Once females have attained puberty, their maximum reproductive output under the standard 22 °C [T = 22 °C] regime is defined by a combination of fecundity per event and annual breeding frequency. Each reproductive event yields an average of 2.96 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2.96 eggs per clutch], and females typically produce a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This reproductive strategy, characterized by a modest clutch size relative to many other whiptail species, likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a parthenogenetic life history, where each offspring is a genetic clone of its mother. The energy invested in producing each egg is substantial, requiring the female to maintain a positive energy balance through active foraging on termites and other small invertebrates throughout the spring and early summer. The annotation of these reproductive parameters allows for a deeper appreciation of the species’ demographic resilience, as even small changes in annual clutch frequency can have profound effects on population growth rates in a species with a relatively short reproductive lifespan.

The ultimate snout-vent length attained by a fully grown adult Chihuahuan spotted whiptail has been documented at approximately 8.65 centimeters [Li = approximately 8.65 centimeters], a measurement that represents the asymptotic size reached after several years of continuous growth. This adult body dimension is broadly consistent with that of other parthenogenetic members of the Aspidoscelis tesselata species complex, suggesting a conserved genetic program governing body size determination. In conjunction with this linear somatic measurement, the corresponding ultimate wet body mass has been recorded at 7.8 grams [Wwi = 7.8 grams], a value that reflects the species’ slender, elongated body plan optimized for rapid movement through the desert scrub understory. The relationship between snout-vent length and body mass in this species follows a predictable power function, with mass increasing approximately as the cube of length, in accordance with general allometric scaling principles. These asymptotic size measurements are critical for calibrating growth models and for comparing the energetic demands of adult maintenance across different populations occupying distinct habitat patches within the species’ fragmented range.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Aspidoscelis exsanguis under favorable conditions maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] is approximately 1,460 days (1460 days) [am = 1460 days], which corresponds to four complete annual cycles. This longevity estimate, derived from mark-recapture studies of captive cohorts and supplemented by field observations of free-ranging individuals, positions the Chihuahuan spotted whiptail as a relatively short-lived lizard compared to some larger iguanian species, yet it is comparable to the lifespans reported for other syntopic teiids. The completion of the natural lifespan is typically marked by a period of reproductive senescence, during which fecundity declines noticeably before the eventual physiological death of the individual. Understanding the species’ maximum longevity is essential for evaluating its susceptibility to environmental perturbations; a brief lifespan means that even a single year of reproductive failure due to drought or habitat alteration can severely impact population persistence. This demographic vulnerability is partially offset by the advantages of parthenogenetic reproduction, where every mature individual is capable of founding a new population without the Allee effects associated with mate limitation.
